state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about this further. Can you explain why you believe the range wouldn't change if all the plants were cut in half or grew by the same amount? How does changing all values by the same proportion affect the spread of the data set?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I think... when you cut all the plants in half, the difference between the biggest and smallest plant gets smaller too, so the range changes. But when you add 3 cm to all of them, the gap between them stays the same, so the range doesn't change? Is that right, or am I still getting it wrong?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track! Can you think of a scenario where changing all values by the same proportion does affect the range? How might this apply to the plants' heights in this situation?

score.justification_pass1: While the student successfully corrects their misconception by Turn 2, the teacher's Turn 3 response is mathematically confusing (asking them to find a scenario where proportional change affects range, when the student just correctly explained it does) and fails to affirm the correct reasoning the student has already demonstrated.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking without giving direct answers, though they could have used a counterexample to more explicitly expose the flaw in the student's initial reasoning about Tom being correct.
